title: Nighthawk random-circuit sampling on 61 qubits
summary: The released 61-qubit depth-36 circuit returned one million bitstrings on IBM Phoenix in 19 registered QPU seconds. A local chi=128 MPS simulation of the same logical circuit took 1,248.95 seconds for 1,000 bitstrings, a 65.7x execution-metric contrast. Its one-bit RMS discrepancy was 0.09047, within an exploratory 0.10 hobby tolerance; process-level fidelity was not independently matched.

comparison.headline: The 19-second QPU usage was 65.7x shorter than a 1,248.95-second local chi=128 MPS simulation of the same released circuit. The MPS one-bit RMS discrepancy of 0.09047 passes an exploratory 0.10 hobby tolerance, but circuit-level fidelity was not matched.
comparison.scope: This is a local execution-metric contrast between hardware and one named circuit-following capped-MPS implementation, not a matched-fidelity time-to-answer result. The provider QPU usage covers one million shots; the local wall time covers 1000 shots.

implementation.access_note: The public repository contains code and article sources. The raw million-shot research data and large binaries were not included in that public release.

claim_boundary: The 0.10 RMS band is an exploratory post-measurement hobby criterion on one-bit probabilities, much looser than the approximately 0.018 noise-only 95% threshold for 1000 shots.
A circuit-independent random-bit generator also passes the one-bit RMS check; it is only a negative control for the check and is not a competitor for simulating the specified quantum process.
The 19-second quantum value is QPU usage and the 1,248.95-second classical value is local simulator wall time; shot counts differ by a factor of 1000 and queue, preparation and analysis are excluded.
Passing the coarse marginal band does not validate the full 61-bit distribution, ideal-circuit fidelity or full-width XEB. No independent full-distribution quality match was measured.

The 65.7x number is a timing lead over one named circuit-following capped-MPS workflow. Without a matched process-fidelity estimate, it is not a demonstrated matched-quality, best-classical, full-distribution or end-to-end quantum advantage.
